analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, counties, and tribes build their own broadband networks even where state laws ban it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2016 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Several states have laws that stop local governments, or in some cases Indian tribes, from offering high-speed internet to residents. This bill would amend federal telecommunications law to say no state can block a public provider from offering broadband. It also requires that when a city runs a network, it must regulate private competitors evenhandedly and stay subject to the same federal and state rules as everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of areas with slow, expensive, or unavailable internet service. Local governments and Indian tribes that want to build their own networks gain the legal right to do so, even in states that currently forbid it. Communities where a single cable or phone company holds a monopoly would get the option of a public alternative.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents with poor or expensive internet service

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars any state statute or rule from prohibiting a public provider—a state, city, county, or Indian tribe—from offering advanced telecommunications capability or services, such as broadband internet.
It adds an anti-discrimination safeguard: a public provider that regulates competing private broadband providers cannot favor itself or a provider it owns.

A savings clause keeps public providers subject to the same federal and state telecommunications laws and regulations that apply to all providers, so the networks do not get a special regulatory carve-out.

analysis.who_pays: Private broadband and cable companies would face new public-sector competition in places they currently serve exclusively or not at all. Taxpayers in a city or county that chooses to build a network bear the financial risk if the venture fails, though the bill leaves standard telecommunications regulation in place and does not fund networks directly.

drawbacks.text: Government-built networks carry financial risk: if a city or county borrows to build a broadband system and it does not attract enough customers, local taxpayers are on the hook for the losses. The bill does not require any feasibility or funding plan before a public provider starts.

The bill overrides state legislative decisions about whether local governments should be in the broadband business, a state-sovereignty objection raised by opponents of similar community broadband proposals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete for people stuck with one slow, expensive internet provider: a legal path for their own local government to build an alternative, with equal-regulation rules attached. The main honest objection is financial risk—if public networks are mismanaged, local taxpayers absorb the loss, and the bill offers no guardrail beyond existing law. On balance the design is reasonably careful (it includes anti-discrimination and equal-regulation provisions), but the bill went nowhere, so the question was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2016, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2017, so it died without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Community Broadband Act of 2016 on September 13, 2016.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over telecommunications law.
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action was taken—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

The bill would have amended the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to bar states from prohibiting public providers of broadband, with anti-discrimination and equal-regulation safeguards for private competitors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent broadband and cable companies are better off, since no law now requires states to allow public competitors. State legislatures that have banned municipal broadband keep those bans. Residents without affordable high-speed internet gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent broadband providers and restricting state legislatures

for.name: Rep. Anna G. Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Broadband Act of 2016 to preserve local governments' ability to provide broadband.

for.name: 2 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; both were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in September 2016 and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or vote—before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cable and telecom incumbents
against.role: Private broadband providers with state laws protecting them from municipal competition
against.what_they_did: Opposed community broadband legislation and supported state restrictions on municipal networks; industry lobbying shaped the committee environment in which the bill received no consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of full House and Senate support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Cable, telecom, and internet service providers
industries.note: The bill would have allowed cities, counties, and tribes to build competing broadband networks, threatening incumbents' exclusive hold on local markets. Where incumbents benefit from a monopoly by charging high prices for slow service, their interest runs against residents seeking cheaper alternatives.

industries.industry: State and local governments and Indian tribes
industries.note: The bill would give states, municipalities, and tribes the legal right to provide broadband even where state law forbids it, letting them serve residents directly or spur competition.
